Neural-network quantum states for the nuclear many-body problem

Journal: Progress in Particle and Nuclear Physics

Abstract

A long-standing goal of nuclear theory is to explain how the structure and dynamics of atomic nuclei and neutron-star matter emerge from the underlying interactions among protons and neutrons. Achieving this goal requires solving the nuclear quantum many-body problem with high accuracy across a wide range of length scales and density regimes. In this review, we discuss how artificial neural network representations of the nuclear many-body wave function have significantly extended the capabilities of continuum quantum Monte Carlo methods. In particular, neural-network quantum states enable calculations of larger systems than were previously accessible and provide a flexible framework for capturing phenomena that challenge conventional approaches, including the emergence of nuclear clusters and superfluid phases in dense matter. We highlight recent applications to finite nuclei, infinite nuclear and neutron matter, and dynamical processes relevant to lepton–nucleus and nucleus–nucleus scattering. We also discuss conceptual and methodological connections with condensed matter physics, emphasizing developments in neural-network quantum states that bridge strongly correlated systems across disciplines. Together, these developments demonstrate how neural-network methods open new avenues toward unified and accurate descriptions of nuclear structure, matter, and reactions.

Keywords: 
Neural Network Quantum States, Nuclear Quantum Many-Body Problem, Atomic Nuclei , Neutron Star Matter , Nuclear Electroweak Interactions

1  Introduction

At the energy scales relevant for the dynamics of atomic nuclei, the fundamental theory of strong interactions, quantum chromodynamics (QCD), becomes non-perturbative, and quarks and gluons are confined within hadrons. Following the seminal works of Weinberg Weinberg [1990], Weinberg [1991], effective field theories (EFTs) have emerged as the framework of choice for computing low-energy nuclear observables with quantified uncertainties. Two prominent examples are pionless EFT and chiral EFT, both of which exploit a separation between a “hard” momentum scale Λ\Lambda and a “soft” scale QQ that characterizes the typical momenta in low-energy nuclear systems Epelbaum et al. [2009a], Machleidt and Entem [2011]. Pionless EFT is applicable when Q≪mπQ\ll m_{\pi}, and its breakdown scale is set by Λ∼mπ\Lambda\sim m_{\pi}. In contrast, chiral EFT retains explicit pion degrees of freedom, and its breakdown scale is considerably higher, Λ∼600\Lambda\sim 600–700700 MeV, while the soft scale remains Q∼mπQ\sim m_{\pi}. At low energies, protons and neutrons interact through nonrelativistic potentials systematically organized as an expansion in Q/ΛQ/\Lambda van Kolck [1994], Epelbaum et al. [2009a], Machleidt and Entem [2011]. High-momentum physics is integrated out and encoded in low-energy constants fitted to nucleon–nucleon scattering data and observables in light nuclei.

Interactions and electroweak currents derived consistently within the EFT framework provide the primary input to ab initio methods designed to solve the nuclear many-body Schrödinger equation with controlled and systematically improvable approximations Hergert [2020], Ekström et al. [2023]. Single-particle basis methods such as the no-core shell model (NCSM) Barrett et al. [2013], coupled-cluster (CC) theory Hagen et al. [2014], the in-medium similarity renormalization group (IMSRG) Hergert et al. [2016], and self-consistent Green’s function (SCGF) techniques Carbone et al. [2013] have achieved impressive success. The NCSM and its resonating-group extension Navratil et al. [2009] accurately describe clustering and collective dynamics Quaglioni and Navratil [2008], Roth et al. [2011], McCoy et al. [2020] but are generally restricted to light nuclei, and convergence for long-range observables can be slow Caprio et al. [2022]. Polynomially scaling approaches such as CC and IMSRG now reach nuclei as heavy as 100Sn Hagen et al. [2016], Morris et al. [2018], Mougeot and others [2021] and 208Pb Hu and others [2022], providing access to spectra, response functions, and transition rates Sobczyk et al. [2021], Acharya et al. [2024], Bonaiti et al. [2024]. These developments have deepened our understanding of the long-standing quenching of gAg_{A} Gysbers and others [2019] and enabled uncertainty-quantified predictions of neutrinoless double-β\beta decay Yao et al. [2020], Wirth et al. [2021], Belley et al. [2021]. Nevertheless, truncation of model spaces limits their ability to fully capture multi-scale phenomena, especially alpha clustering and short-range correlations. Symmetry-adapted shell-model approaches Launey et al. [2016], Dytrych et al. [2020] mitigate some of these challenges but they may not be able to fully capture short-distance dynamics.

A second class of ab initio methods relies on stochastic formulations, such as nuclear lattice EFT (NLEFT) Lee [2025] and continuum quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) techniques Carlson et al. [2015], Lynn et al. [2019], Gandolfi et al. [2020]. NLEFT has advanced to medium-mass nuclei Elhatisari and others [2024], revealing compelling signatures of alpha clustering Shen et al. [2023] and providing insights into nuclear matter at finite temperature Ren et al. [2024], Ma et al. [2024], enabled by substantial algorithmic progress Sarkar et al. [2023]. However, the fermion sign problem and the computational cost of fine lattice spacings limit its ability to resolve short-range dynamics with high accuracy. Continuum QMC methods, such as Green’s function Monte Carlo (GFMC) Carlson [1988] and auxiliary-field diffusion Monte Carlo (AFDMC) Schmidt and Fantoni [1999], accurately describe nuclear dynamics across long, intermediate, and short ranges. In practice, however, GFMC scales exponentially with the mass number, restricting applications to nuclei with A≲13A\lesssim 13, while AFDMC encounters a severe sign problem when realistic correlations are introduced, limiting its applicability to nuclei with A∼16A\sim 16 Novario et al. [2023], Martin et al. [2023].

These challenges have motivated the exploration of neural-network representations of quantum many-body wave functions, a framework that has already achieved notable success in condensed-matter physics and quantum chemistry Carleo and Troyer [2017], Hermann et al. [2020], Pfau et al. [2020]. In the nuclear domain, however, neural-network quantum states (NQS) methods face a distinct set of difficulties. Nuclear interactions are highly non-perturbative and exhibit strong spin–isospin dependence, placing them well outside the regime where mean-field approximations provide a reliable starting point Wiringa et al. [1995]. As a result, NQS methods are confronted with correlations at all length scales. At the same time, realistic nuclear Hamiltonians require treating both continuous spatial degrees of freedom and discrete spin and isospin degrees of freedom, significantly enlarging the structure of the underlying Hilbert space.

In this review, we discuss the development and application of NQS ansätze in nuclear physics and closely related areas. Following the pioneering application of NQS to the deuteron Keeble and Rios [2020], variational Monte Carlo methods based on NQS Adams et al. [2021], Yang and Zhao [2022], Lovato et al. [2022b], Yang and Zhao [2023], Gnech et al. [2024] have proven to provide a systematically improvable framework with polynomial computational scaling and have begun to address several long-standing challenges in ab initio nuclear theory. Our focus is on first-quantized architectures, which operate directly on the continuous spatial coordinates and discrete spin–isospin degrees of freedom of the nucleons. This representation naturally accommodates short-, intermediate-, and long-range nuclear dynamics, from the repulsive core and tensor correlations to clustering and collective degrees of freedom. Moreover, NQS approaches capture the multiscale behavior characteristic of nuclei and neutron-star matter Fore et al. [2023], including superfluidity, the emergence of nuclear clusters, and dominant short-range correlations Kim et al. [2024], Fore et al. [2024].

First, we briefly review existing continuum QMC methods, focusing in particular on GFMC and the computational challenges associated with treating nuclei with more than A=13A=13 nucleons. This naturally leads to a discussion on how the Hilbert space is sampled in VMC methods, with emphasis on the nuclear case, where both continuous (spatial coordinates) and discrete (spin–isospin) degrees of freedom must be sampled efficiently. After providing a short recap of the elements of deep learning relevant to NQS approaches, we introduce the main first-quantized NQS architectures proposed to date and discuss how physical symmetries—such as parity, time-reversal, and translation invariance—are incorporated into these models.

In the second part of the review, we summarize the most important recent results for finite nuclei and for infinite nuclear and neutron matter. We then discuss initial applications of NQS wave functions to lepton–nucleus and nucleus–nucleus scattering, highlighting the potential of these methods to deliver unified and accurate ab initio descriptions of both nuclear structure and reactions, and to extend the reach of nuclear many-body theory beyond the traditional limits imposed by basis truncations and the sign problem. Before concluding, we provide a selective overview NQS approaches to condensed matter theory, focusing particularly on those that have direct links to nuclear theory.

2  The nuclear quantum many-body problem

The nuclear quantum many-body problem presents formidable challenges due to the strong spin–isospin dependence and intrinsically non-perturbative character of realistic nuclear interactions. In contrast to quantum chemistry, where the Coulomb interaction is known a priori and provides a universal two-body potential, nuclear forces must be derived within the EFT framework. The construction of accurate two- and three-nucleon interactions with quantified uncertainties remains an active research frontier Epelbaum et al. [2009a], Machleidt and Entem [2011], Ekström et al. [2023].

Recent advances in Bayesian parameter estimation and regulator optimization have further improved the consistency and predictive power of modern chiral EFT Hamiltonians. The complexity of these interactions has motivated the development of a broad suite of ab initio many-body approaches Hergert [2020]. Single-particle basis methods, including the NCSM, CC theory, SCGF and the IMSRG, have achieved high-precision results across wide regions of the nuclear chart. Complementary stochastic formulations such as NLEFT have revealed striking signatures of clustering Shen et al. [2023] and have advanced toward medium-mass nuclei, though their finite lattice spacing limits the resolution of short-range dynamics. Continuum QMC methods Carlson et al. [2015], Lynn et al. [2019], Gandolfi et al. [2020], including GFMC Carlson [1988] and AFDMC Schmidt and Fantoni [1999], accurately capture nuclear dynamics from long to short distances, but their applicability across the nuclear chart remains restricted. GFMC scales exponentially with the mass number, while AFDMC suffers from a worsening sign problem for realistic chiral interactions Novario et al. [2023], Martin et al. [2023].

Because this review focuses on neural quantum states (NQS) applied to continuum QMC, this section summarizes the local coordinate-space Hamiltonians derived from EFT that serve as inputs to both conventional QMC and NQS-based VMC calculations Gezerlis et al. [2014]. We then discuss the principal scaling bottlenecks encountered by GFMC and AFDMC as the mass number increases, highlighting the aspects most relevant for constructing efficient NQS ansätze. These considerations motivate the exploration of first-quantized NQS architectures that act directly on the continuous spatial coordinates and discrete spin–isospin degrees of freedom, offering a promising path toward extending the reach of continuum QMC methods beyond their traditional limits.

2.1  Nuclear Hamiltonian

To a remarkable extent, the properties of atomic nuclei and neutron-star matter can be described by point-like nucleons whose dynamics are governed by a nonrelativistic Hamiltonian

HL​O\displaystyle H_{LO} =∑i𝐩i22​mN+∑i<jvi​j+∑i<j<kVi​j​k,\displaystyle=\sum_{i}\frac{\mathbf{p}_{i}^{2}}{2m_{N}}+\sum_{i<j}v_{ij}+\sum_{i<j<k}V_{ijk}\,, (2.1)

where 𝐩i\mathbf{p}_{i} is the three-momentum of the ii-th nucleon, mNm_{N} is its mass, and vi​jv_{ij} and Vi​j​kV_{ijk} are the potentials describing nucleon-nucleon (N​NN\!N) and three-nucleon (3​N3N) interactions, respectively.

With the notable exception of Ref. Keeble and Rios [2020], and more recently Refs. Wen et al. [2025], Yang et al. [2025a], most applications of neural quantum states (NQS) to nuclear physics employ N​NN\!N and 3​N3N potentials based on the premise that the momentum scales relevant for modeling the structure of atomic nuclei are much smaller than the pion mass, mπ≃140m_{\pi}\simeq 140 MeV. In this regime, pions can be integrated out, giving rise to pionless EFT Chen et al. [1999], Bedaque and van Kolck [2002], in which the charge-independent (CI) nuclear interactions consist solely of contact terms between two or more nucleons. Pionless EFT provides a controlled and systematically improvable description of nuclear systems in the low-momentum regime, where short-range correlations and universal behavior dominate the structure of light nuclei and dilute nuclear matter. At the same time, its reduced operator complexity offers a natural setting for developing and benchmarking first-quantized NQS architectures, allowing one to isolate representational and optimization challenges before confronting the additional multiscale structure and strong tensor correlations induced by explicit pion exchange.

In this review, we focus on the leading-order (LO) pionless EFT expansion of Ref. Schiavilla et al. [2021]. The LO N​NN\!N interaction derived in that work is constrained to act only in even partial waves. In coordinate space, it is given by

vL​OC​I​(ri​j)=C01​C1​(ri​j)​P0σ​P1τ+C10​C0​(ri​j)​P1σ​P0τ,v_{LO}^{CI}(r_{ij})=C_{01}C_{1}(r_{ij})P_{0}^{\sigma}P_{1}^{\tau}+C_{10}C_{0}(r_{ij})P_{1}^{\sigma}P_{0}^{\tau}, (2.2)

where ri​j=|𝐫i−𝐫j|r_{ij}=|{\bf r}_{i}-{\bf r}_{j}| and P0,1σP_{0,1}^{\sigma} (P0,1τP_{0,1}^{\tau}) are the spin (isospin) projection operators for the nucleon pair i​jij with total spin SS and isospin TT equal to 0 or 1:

P0σ=1−σi​j4,P1σ=3+σi​j4,P0τ=1−τi​j4,P1τ=3+τi​j4.P_{0}^{\sigma}=\frac{1-\sigma_{ij}}{4},\qquad P_{1}^{\sigma}=\frac{3+\sigma_{ij}}{4},\qquad P_{0}^{\tau}=\frac{1-\tau_{ij}}{4},\qquad P_{1}^{\tau}=\frac{3+\tau_{ij}}{4}\,. (2.3)

Here, σi​j=𝝈i⋅𝝈j\sigma_{ij}={\boldsymbol{\sigma}}_{i}\cdot{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}_{j} and τi​j=𝝉i⋅𝝉j\tau_{ij}={\boldsymbol{\tau}}_{i}\cdot{\boldsymbol{\tau}}_{j}, with 𝝈i{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}_{i} and 𝝉i{\boldsymbol{\tau}}_{i} denoting the Pauli spin and isospin operators acting on nucleon ii, respectively. In this implementation, the contact interactions are regularized using Gaussian cutoff functions,

Cα​(r)=1π3/2​Rα3​e−(r/Rα)2,C_{\alpha}(r)=\frac{1}{\pi^{3/2}R_{\alpha}^{3}}\,e^{-(r/R_{\alpha})^{2}}, (2.4)

where RαR_{\alpha} controls the range of the regulator.

Most of the results presented in this review are obtained using model “o” of Ref. Schiavilla et al. [2021], in which the cutoff radii R0=1.5459R_{0}=1.5459 fm and R1=1.8304R_{1}=1.8304 fm, as well as the low-energy constants C01=−5.27518671C_{01}=-5.27518671 fm2 and C10=−7.04040080C_{10}=-7.04040080 fm2, were adjusted to reproduce the neutron–proton scattering lengths and effective ranges in the singlet and triplet channels, as well as the deuteron binding energy. To demonstrate the performance of this interaction, Fig. 2.1 displays the phase shifts in the S13{}^{3}S_{1} and S01{}^{1}S_{0} channels for n​pnp scattering.

On the one hand, we observe excellent agreement with both the PWA93 analysis and those obtained from the highly realistic Argonne v18 potential, extending up to Tlab=5T_{\rm lab}=5 MeV. On the other hand, the phase shifts of the model “o” in the S01{}^{1}S_{0} channels for p​ppp and n​nnn scattering, displayed in Fig. 2.2, exhibit some discrepancies compared to both the PWA93 analysis and those obtained from the realistic Argonne v18 potential Wiringa et al. [1995]. These differences can be attributed to the absence of a charge-dependent term in model “o”, which enters at next-to-leading order (NLO) in the pionless EFT expansion. It has yet to be determined whether including these terms will stabilize 6He, 8Li, 8B, 9C, and 17F against breakup into smaller clusters, or if P-wave terms need to be incorporated into the nucleon-nucleon interaction Gattobigio et al. [2019].

The N​NN\!N potential of Eq. (2.2) can be expressed compactly in the spin–isospin operator basis as

vi​jCI=∑p=14vp​(ri​j)​Oi​jp,\displaystyle v^{\rm CI}_{ij}=\sum_{p=1}^{4}v^{p}(r_{ij})O^{p}_{ij}\,, (2.5)

where Oi​jp=1,4=(1,τi​j,σi​j,σi​j​τi​j)O^{p=1,4}_{ij}=\bigl(1,\tau_{ij},\sigma_{ij},\sigma_{ij}\tau_{ij}\bigr), akin to the v4′v_{4}^{\prime} potential Wiringa and Pieper [2002]. The explicit forms of the radial functions vp​(ri​j)v^{p}(r_{ij}) are provided in Appendix A of Ref. Schiavilla et al. [2021], and their radial dependence is illustrated in Fig. 2.3.

In addition to the CI component, the two-nucleon interaction includes an electromagnetic (EM) contribution, such that v=vEM+vLOCIv=v^{\rm EM}+v^{\rm CI}_{\rm LO}. The full vEMv^{\rm EM} consists of one- and two-photon Coulomb terms, the Darwin-Foldy term, vacuum polarization, and magnetic moment interactions; see Ref. Wiringa et al. [1995] for their explicit expressions. However, most NQS applications retain only the Coulomb repulsion between finite-size (rather than point-like) protons.

In pionless EFT, solving systems with A≥3A\geq 3 using purely attractive LO N​NN\!N potentials leads to the so-called Thomas collapse Yang [2020] as the regulator is removed. This pathological behavior is avoided by promoting a contact 3​N3N force to LO Bedaque et al. [1999]. In this review, we consider a regularized 3​N3N potential of the form

Vi​j​k=cEfπ4​Λχ(ℏ​c)6π3​R36∑cyce−(ri​j2+rj​k2)/R32,\displaystyle V_{ijk}=\frac{c_{E}}{f_{\pi}^{4}\Lambda_{\chi}}\frac{(\hbar c)^{6}}{\pi^{3}R_{3}^{6}}\sum_{\rm cyc}e^{-(r_{ij}^{2}+r_{jk}^{2})/R_{3}^{2}}, (2.6)

where Λχ=1\Lambda_{\chi}=1 GeV, fπ=92.4f_{\pi}=92.4 MeV is the pion decay constant, and ∑cyc\sum_{\rm cyc} denotes cyclic permutations of the indices ii, jj, and kk. The low-energy constant cEc_{E} is fixed to reproduce the 3H binding energy, B(3B(^{3}HOPEN)=8.475)=8.475 MeV, for a given value of the cutoff R3R_{3}. The analysis of Ref. Schiavilla et al. [2021] shows that the choice R3=1.0R_{3}=1.0 fm and cE=1.0786c_{E}=1.0786 provides a satisfactory description of nuclear binding energies across a broad mass range, up to 90Zr. However, subsequent VMC–NQS calculations have indicated that this choice leads to overbinding in 16O and heavier nuclei. Increasing the cutoff to R3=1.1R_{3}=1.1 fm with cE=1.2945c_{E}=1.2945 largely resolves this issue Gnech et al. [2024], as the extended range of the 3​N3N force introduces additional repulsion in heavier systems.

Very recent applications of nuclear NQS employ higher-resolution interactions, either phenomenological or derived within chiral EFT. In particular, Refs. Yang et al. [2025b], Wen et al. [2025], Yang et al. [2025a] use consistent N​NNN and 3​N3N potentials derived at next-to-next-to-leading order (N2LO) in the chiral EFT expansion that are local in coordinate space Gezerlis et al. [2013], Gezerlis et al. [2014], Lynn et al. [2016]. Notably, the authors of Ref. Yang et al. [2025b] were also able to employ NQS with the phenomenological Argonne v8′v_{8}^{\prime} + Urbana IX Hamiltonian Pudliner et al. [1995], which features a strongly repulsive core at short distances. The charge-independent (CI) part of both the Argonne v8′v_{8}^{\prime} interaction and the local N2LO chiral EFT potentials can be written in operator form as

vi​j=∑p=18vp​(ri​j)​Oi​jp,v_{ij}=\sum_{p=1}^{8}v^{p}(r_{ij})O^{p}_{ij}\,, (2.7)

where ri​j=|𝐫i−𝐫j|r_{ij}=|{\bf r}_{i}-{\bf r}_{j}| is the interparticle distance. For the local N2LO chiral EFT potential, the sum is restricted to the first seven operators. Compared to Eq. (2.5), the additional operators entering this expansion include the tensor and spin-orbit components, for a total of eight operators, where Oi​jp=5,8=(Si​j,Si​j​τi​j,𝐋⋅𝐒,𝐋⋅𝐒​τi​j)O^{p=5,8}_{ij}=\bigl(S_{ij},S_{ij}\,\tau_{ij},\mathbf{L}\cdot\mathbf{S},\mathbf{L}\cdot\mathbf{S}\,\tau_{ij}\bigr). The tensor operator is

Si​j=3ri​j2​(𝝈i⋅𝐫i​j)​(𝝈j⋅𝐫i​j)−σi​j,S_{ij}=\frac{3}{r^{2}_{ij}}(\boldsymbol{\sigma}_{i}\cdot{\bf r}_{ij})(\boldsymbol{\sigma}_{j}\cdot{\bf r}_{ij})-\sigma_{ij}\,, (2.8)

while the spin-orbit contribution is expressed in terms of the relative angular momentum 𝐋=12​i​(𝐫i−𝐫j)×(∇i−∇j)\mathbf{L}=\frac{1}{2i}(\mathbf{r}_{i}-\mathbf{r}_{j})\times(\nabla_{i}-\nabla_{j}) and the total spin 𝐒=12​(𝝈i+𝝈j)\mathbf{S}=\frac{1}{2}(\boldsymbol{\sigma}_{i}+\boldsymbol{\sigma}_{j}) of the pair. The radial functions of the Argonne v8′v_{8}^{\prime} potential are displayed in Fig. 2.4. In contrast to the model “o” interaction of Fig. 2.3, the Argonne potential exhibits a very strong short-range repulsive core, exceeding 2 GeV (in the figure the central channel is divided by a factor of 5 for visibility). The sizable tensor and spin–orbit components, which extend to relatively large distances, are also clearly visible. This long-range behavior is a consequence of one-pion exchange. While the associated tensor interaction is singular at short distances in its bare form, scaling as 1/r31/r^{3}, this divergence is regularized in the Argonne interaction. The interaction nevertheless remains long-ranged in the Yukawa sense at large separations, decaying as e−mπ​r/re^{-m_{\pi}r}/r up to polynomial factors, and provides the dominant source of tensor correlations at intermediate distances in nuclei. Note that the Coulomb interaction, which is the longest-ranged component of the nuclear Hamiltonian, decays as 1/r1/r but is comparatively weak and acts only between protons.

The earliest example of a 3​N3N force dates back to the Fujita–Miyazawa interaction, whose main contributions arise from the virtual excitation of a Δ⁡(1232)\Delta(1232) resonance in processes involving three interacting nucleons Fujita and Miyazawa [1957]. This term is included in both chiral EFT and in the Urbana IX potential Pudliner et al. [1995] and reads

Vi​j​kΔ=Vi​j​kΔ,a+Vi​j​kΔ,c.V_{ijk}^{\Delta}=V_{ijk}^{\Delta,a}+V_{ijk}^{\Delta,c}\,. (2.9)

The “anticommutator” and “commutator” contributions are

Vi​j​kΔ,a=∑cycA2​π​{Xi​jπ,Xj​kπ}​{τi​j,τj​k},Vi​j​kΔ,c=∑cycC2​π​[Xi​jπ,Xj​kπ]​[τi​j,τj​k],V_{ijk}^{\Delta,a}=\sum_{\rm cyc}A_{2\pi}\,\{X_{ij}^{\pi},X_{jk}^{\pi}\}\,\{\tau_{ij},\tau_{jk}\}\quad,\quad V_{ijk}^{\Delta,c}=\sum_{\rm cyc}C_{2\pi}\,[X_{ij}^{\pi},X_{jk}^{\pi}]\,[\tau_{ij},\tau_{jk}]\,, (2.10)

where ∑cyc\sum_{\rm cyc} denotes a sum over the three cyclic permutations of the nucleons i,j,ki,j,k. The operator Xi​jπX_{ij}^{\pi} is defined as

Xi​jπ=T⁡(ri​j)​Si​j+Y⁡(ri​j)​σi​j,X_{ij}^{\pi}=T(r_{ij})\,S_{ij}+Y(r_{ij})\,\sigma_{ij}\,, (2.11)

where the radial Yukawa and tensor functions, Y⁡(r)Y(r) and T⁡(r)T(r), are defined consistently with those appearing in the corresponding N​NNN interaction Wiringa et al. [1995], Pudliner et al. [1997].

Generally, a three-body potential composed only of Vi​j​kΔV_{ijk}^{\Delta} does not reproduce the empirical saturation density of isospin-symmetric nucleonic matter Lagaris and Pandharipande [1981]; a repulsive three-body contribution must be included,

Vi​j​kR=AR​∑cycT2​(ri​j)​T2​(rj​k).V^{R}_{ijk}=A_{R}\sum_{\rm cyc}T^{2}(r_{ij})\,T^{2}(r_{jk})\,. (2.12)

The constants A2​πA_{2\pi} and ARA_{R} entering the Urbana IX model are determined by fitting the binding energy of 3H and the saturation density of isospin-symmetric nucleonic matter, ρ0=0.16​fm−3\rho_{0}=0.16~\mathrm{fm}^{-3} Akmal et al. [1998]. Chiral EFT interactions likewise include a short-range three-body operator proportional to the low-energy constant cEc_{E}. This contribution may be purely scalar or contain isospin dependence, although the latter appears to be incompatible with astrophysical constraints.

In addition to the terms above, chiral EFT three-body forces at N2LO contain a one-pion-exchange (OPE) three-body component proportional to the low-energy constant cDc_{D}, as well as a second short-range contact proportional to cEc_{E}. The OPE three-body structure is also included in the phenomenological Illinois-7 force Pieper [2008]. For detailed discussions of these terms, we refer the reader to Refs. Lynn et al. [2017], while Ref. Lovato et al. [2012] provides a comprehensive comparison between local phenomenological and chiral EFT interactions.

2.2  Progress and challenges of quantum Monte Carlo methods

The Hamiltonians discussed in the previous section are the main input to ab initio many-body methods that, within controlled approximations, solve the nuclear Schrödinger equation

H⁡|Ψn⟩=En​|Ψn⟩,H|\Psi_{n}\rangle=E_{n}|\Psi_{n}\rangle\,, (2.13)

where |Ψn⟩|\Psi_{n}\rangle denotes the nnth eigenstate and EnE_{n} its associated eigenvalue. Several stochastic many-body frameworks have been developed to address this problem. Two broad and complementary approaches are lattice formulations based on path-integral methods and continuum quantum Monte Carlo techniques.

Nuclear lattice effective field theory (NLEFT) Epelbaum et al. [2011], Lee [2025], aided by notable algorithmic advances Sarkar et al. [2023], has expanded its reach to medium-mass nuclei Elhatisari and others [2024], provided compelling evidence for α\alpha clustering Shen et al. [2023], and explored nuclear and neutron matter at finite temperature Ren et al. [2024], Ma et al. [2024]. However, NLEFT continues to face limitations arising from the fermion sign problem and the rapidly growing computational cost associated with fine lattice spacings, which constrain its ability to resolve short-range dynamics unless simplified interactions are used.

Continuum QMC methods Carlson et al. [2015], Gandolfi et al. [2020], originally developed in condensed-matter physics and later adapted to nuclear systems, operate directly in coordinate space. The variational Monte Carlo (VMC) method optimizes a parametrized trial state to capture the most important correlations and enforce the correct asymptotic behavior, thereby accurately describing long-range dynamics and α\alpha clustering. Building on VMC, Green’s function Monte Carlo (GFMC) Carlson [1987], Carlson [1988] projects the variational state in imaginary time toward exact eigenstates, while auxiliary-field diffusion Monte Carlo (AFDMC) Schmidt and Fantoni [1999] employs Hubbard–Stratonovich auxiliary fields to sample spin–isospin operators and access larger systems. These continuum approaches model nuclear dynamics across long, intermediate, and short distances and can accommodate “stiff” interactions with high-momentum components. Recent applications include ground-state properties Piarulli and others [2018], inclusive electron- and neutrino-scattering Lovato et al. [2020], Andreoli et al. [2024], and a variety of electroweak observables such as electromagnetic moments and form factors, low-energy transitions and β\beta decays, and muon-capture processes King et al. [2023], Chambers-Wall et al. [2024].

In this review, we focus primarily on the VMC method, first outlining the computational challenges of conventional variational states. VMC relies on the Rayleigh–Ritz variational principle

⟨ΨV​(𝜽)|H|ΨV​(𝜽)⟩⟨ΨV​(𝜽)|ΨV​(𝜽)⟩≡EV​(𝜽)≥E0\frac{\langle\Psi_{V}(\boldsymbol{\theta})\,|\,H\,|\,\Psi_{V}(\boldsymbol{\theta})\rangle}{\langle\Psi_{V}(\boldsymbol{\theta})\,|\,\Psi_{V}(\boldsymbol{\theta})\rangle}\equiv E_{V}(\boldsymbol{\theta})\geq E_{0} (2.14)

to determine the optimal set of parameters 𝜽\boldsymbol{\theta} defining the variational state ΨV\Psi_{V}. For the nuclear many-body problem, it is customary to assume that the trial state factorizes into long- and short-range components,

ΨV(R,S)≡⟨R,S|ΨV⟩=⟨RS|(1+∑i<j<kFi​j​k)(𝒮∏i<jFi​j)|Φ⟩,\Psi_{V}(R,S)\equiv\langle R,S\,|\Psi_{V}\rangle=\langle RS\,|\left(1+\sum_{i<j<k}F_{ijk}\right)\left(\mathcal{S}\prod_{i<j}F_{ij}\right)|\Phi\rangle\,, (2.15)

where Fi​jF_{ij} and Fi​j​kF_{ijk} are two- and three-body correlation operators, respectively. The symbol 𝒮\mathcal{S} denotes a symmetrized product over nucleon pairs, since—in general, owing to their spin–isospin dependence—the Fi​jF_{ij} need not commute. The symbol RR denotes the spatial coordinates of all nucleons, (𝐫1,…,𝐫A)(\mathbf{r}_{1},\ \dots\ ,\ \mathbf{r}_{A}), while SS stands for the spin–isospin degrees of freedom, to be discussed in detail below.

The long-range antisymmetric part Φ\Phi is commonly expressed as a linear combination of a few Slater determinants built from single-particle orbitals appropriate to the system of interest. For homogeneous matter, the orbitals are usually plane waves and may include pairing correlations Gandolfi et al. [2009b]. For atomic nuclei, the single-particle orbitals are generally taken in the l​sls- or j​jjj-coupling schemes and combined to yield the desired total angular momentum JJ and parity PP of the nucleus Pudliner et al. [1997]. Importantly, VMC calculations can explicitly incorporate the strong α\alpha-cluster structure of light nuclei: the wave function of pp-shell systems is constructed as a sum of independent-particle components, each with four nucleons in an α\alpha-like core and the remaining (A−4)(A-4) nucleons occupying pp-shell orbitals Pieper et al. [2002].

The spin–isospin structure of the two-body correlation operator mirrors that of the N​NNN potential and is written as

Fi​j=∑p=16fp​(ri​j)​Oi​jp.F_{ij}=\sum_{p=1}^{6}f^{p}(r_{ij})O^{p}_{ij}. (2.16)

Spin-orbit correlations, corresponding to p=7p=7, 88, may also be included, but are often neglected due to the significant computational cost and the relatively small gain in variational energy Lonardoni et al. [2017]. The optimal radial functions fp​(r)f^{p}(r) are typically obtained by minimizing the two-body cluster contribution to the ground-state energy, subject to the correct asymptotic behavior Lomnitz-Adler et al. [1981]. Appropriate three-body correlation form factors have been derived within perturbation theory, as discussed in Ref. Carlson et al. [2015],

Fi​j​k=∑xϵx​Vi​j​kx​(r~i​j,r~i​k,r~j​k),F_{ijk}=\sum_{x}\epsilon_{x}V_{ijk}^{x}(\tilde{r}_{ij},\tilde{r}_{ik},\tilde{r}_{jk}), (2.17)

where r~=yx​r\tilde{r}=y_{x}r, with yxy_{x} a variational scaling parameter and ϵx\epsilon_{x} a small (negative) strength parameter, both optimized variationally. The superscript xx labels the different components of the three-nucleon interaction (e.g., Δ\Delta, RR).

Both the VMC and GFMC methods employ an explicit many-body basis for the spin–isospin sector of the Hilbert space. A generic basis state can be written as |S⟩≡|χis⟩⊗|χit⟩,|S\rangle\equiv|\chi_{i_{s}}\rangle\otimes|\chi_{i_{t}}\rangle, where the indices isi_{s} and iti_{t} enumerate the many-body spin and isospin basis states, respectively. The 2A2^{A} spin basis states can be written as

|χ1⟩\displaystyle|\chi_{1}\rangle =|↓1,↓2,…,↓A⟩,\displaystyle=|\downarrow_{1},\downarrow_{2},\dots,\downarrow_{A}\rangle,
|χ2⟩\displaystyle|\chi_{2}\rangle =|↑1,↓2,…,↓A⟩,\displaystyle=|\uparrow_{1},\downarrow_{2},\dots,\downarrow_{A}\rangle,
⋮\displaystyle\ \vdots
|χns⟩\displaystyle|\chi_{n_{s}}\rangle =|↑1,↑2,…,↑A⟩,\displaystyle=|\uparrow_{1},\uparrow_{2},\dots,\uparrow_{A}\rangle\,, (2.18)

with ns=2An_{s}=2^{A}. The corresponding isospin states |χit⟩|\chi_{i_{t}}\rangle are obtained by replacing ↓\downarrow with nn and ↑\uparrow with pp. For fixed proton number ZZ (charge conservation), the dimension of the isospin basis is (AZ)\binom{A}{Z}. Figure 2.5 shows the spin–isospin Hilbert-space dimension for nuclei treated with GFMC to date. Data shown includes 13C, currently being computed on ALCF’s Aurora supercomputer, and 16C, anticipated to be within reach of the next generation of leadership-class machines.

The symmetrized product of pair correlation operators is evaluated by successive operations for each pair, sampling their ordering. As an example, consider the application of the operators σ12​σ13​σ23\sigma_{12}\sigma_{13}\sigma_{23} on the three-body spin state |↑1,↓2,↓3⟩|\uparrow_{1},\downarrow_{2},\downarrow_{3}\rangle. Noting that σi​j=2​Pi​jσ−1\sigma_{ij}=2P^{\sigma}_{ij}-1, where 2​Pi​jσ2P^{\sigma}_{ij} exchanges the spin of particles ii and jj, we obtain:

σ12σ13σ23|↑1,↑2,↓3⟩\displaystyle\sigma_{12}\,\sigma_{13}\,\sigma_{23}|\uparrow_{1},\uparrow_{2},\downarrow_{3}\rangle =σ12σ13(2|↑1,↓2,↑3⟩−|↑1,↑2,↓3⟩)\displaystyle=\sigma_{12}\,\sigma_{13}(2|\uparrow_{1},\downarrow_{2},\uparrow_{3}\rangle-|\uparrow_{1},\uparrow_{2},\downarrow_{3}\rangle)
=σ12(2|↑1,↓2,↑3⟩−2|↓1,↑2,↑3⟩+|↑1,↑2,↓3⟩)\displaystyle=\sigma_{12}\,(2|\uparrow_{1},\downarrow_{2},\uparrow_{3}\rangle-2|\downarrow_{1},\uparrow_{2},\uparrow_{3}\rangle+|\uparrow_{1},\uparrow_{2},\downarrow_{3}\rangle)
=4|↓1,↑2,↑3⟩−6|↑1,↓2,↑3⟩−2|↓1,↑2,↑3⟩+|↑1,↑2,↓3⟩).\displaystyle=4|\downarrow_{1},\uparrow_{2},\uparrow_{3}\rangle-6|\uparrow_{1},\downarrow_{2},\uparrow_{3}\rangle-2|\downarrow_{1},\uparrow_{2},\uparrow_{3}\rangle+|\uparrow_{1},\uparrow_{2},\downarrow_{3}\rangle)\,. (2.19)

Hence, even starting from a single spin state, the action of the correlation operator generates four of them (even more are generated by the tensor correlations). In general, the the number of operations necessary to calculate the wave function grows exponentially with the number of nucleons, limiting the applicability of the VMC and GFMC methods to A≤13A\leq 13 nuclei. Sampling the spin–isospin state and evaluating variational wave functions for that sampled state still requires a number of operations that is exponential in the particle number, bringing little savings in terms of computing time Carlson et al. [2015], Gandolfi et al. [2020]. For this reason, both VMC and GFMC are limited to relatively small mass numbers, up to A≃13A\simeq 13.

To circumvent this difficulty, the authors of Ref. Gandolfi et al. [2014] developed a linearized version of the correlator in Eq. (2.15), in which the spin–isospin-independent correlations are retained in full, while the spin–isospin-dependent ones are kept only to first order:

(𝒮​∏i<j∑p=16fp​(ri​j)​Oi​jp)⟶(∏i<jfc​(ri​j))​(1+∑i<j∑p=16up​(ri​j),Oi​jp),\left(\mathcal{S}\prod_{i<j}\sum_{p=1}^{6}f^{p}(r_{ij})O^{p}_{ij}\right)\longrightarrow\left(\prod_{i<j}f^{c}(r_{ij})\right)\left(1+\sum_{i<j}\sum_{p=1}^{6}u^{p}(r_{ij}),O^{p}_{ij}\right)\,, (2.20)

where up​(ri​j)≡fp​(ri​j)/fc​(ri​j)u^{p}(r_{ij})\equiv f^{p}(r_{ij})/f^{c}(r_{ij}). Because only linear terms in the spin–isospin-dependent two-body correlations are kept, this wave function is significantly cheaper to evaluate for a single spin–isospin amplitude than the full product of spin–isospin-dependent two-body correlations. This approach scalie as A5A^{5} rather than exponentially. However, since only pairs of nucleons are correlated at a time, the cluster property is violated. Here, the cluster property means that, for two widely separated groups of nucleons the many-body wave function factorizes, Ψ⁡(A∪B)→Ψ⁡(A)​Ψ​(B)\Psi(A\cup B)\to\Psi(A)\Psi(B), so that connected cross-cluster correlations (and mixed contributions to extensive observables) should vanish.

Nevertheless, the use of these linearized spin-dependent correlations has enabled AFDMC calculations of properties of nuclei up to A∼20A\sim 20 with local chiral EFT interactions. However, the decreasing accuracy with system size prevents the application of AFDMC to medium-mass nuclei, as the method relies on accurate variational wave functions to control the fermion sign problem Piarulli et al. [2020]. To address this issue, the AFDMC variational wave function has been improved by incorporating quadratic pair correlations Lonardoni et al. [2018], at a substantially higher computational cost that scales as A7A^{7}. These increased costs, together with residual violations of the cluster property, substantially limit the current reach of AFDMC, with current applications around A∼16A\sim 16 Novario et al. [2023], Martin et al. [2023].

Extending VMC to larger nuclei calls for variational ansätze that capture the key physics, including short- and long-range correlations, clustering, correct asymptotics, and symmetries, while keeping the computational cost polynomial in AA. This motivates the development of nuclear neural-network quantum states, which provide compact, flexible parameterizations of many-body wave functions and can be optimized efficiently within VMC.

3  Neural-network quantum states for nuclear physics

In recent years, VMC methods leveraging NQS have been developed to model the wave functions of complex nuclear systems with high accuracy and favorable polynomial scaling with the number of nucleons. Similar to conventional continuum QMC methods, working in coordinate space enables NQS-based approaches to efficiently capture short-range nuclear dynamics. As illustrated schematically in Fig. 3.1, NQS architectures typically take as input the spatial and spin-isospin coordinates of the nucleons and output the amplitude and phase of the quantum many-body wave function. A generic neural-network architecture with this construction will not guarantee fermion anti-symmetry, so it must be explicitly imposed. To this aim, in parallel with condensed-matter and quantum-chemistry applications, different ansätze, discussed in detail in Section 3.4, have been developed.

In contrast, in second-quantized approaches, fermion antisymmetry is encoded directly by the basis and the operator algebra: states are expanded in the ordered occupation basis, and fermionic signs follow from the canonical anticommutation relations upon reordering operators. Consequently, in second quantization no additional permutation constraint is imposed on the variational wave function. The fermionic signs are determined by the ordered Fock basis and the anticommutation relations, not by any symmetry of the coefficients Choo et al. [2020].

3.1  Sampling the Hilbert space

Evaluating the variational energy in Eq. (2.14) requires carrying out a 3​A3A-dimensional integral over the continuous Cartesian coordinates of the nucleons, R=(𝐫1,…,𝐫A)R=(\mathbf{r}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{r}_{A}), and a sum over the 2A​(AZ)2^{A}\binom{A}{Z} discrete spin–isospin configurations, S=((s1z,t1z),…,(sAz,tAz)),S=\big((s_{1}^{z},t_{1}^{z}),\ldots,(s_{A}^{z},t_{A}^{z})\big), with sizs_{i}^{z} and tizt_{i}^{z} denoting the spin and isospin projections of the iith nucleon:

EV=⟨ΨV|H|ΨV⟩⟨ΨV|ΨV⟩=∑S∫d​R​⟨ΨV|R​S⟩​⟨R​S|H|ΨV⟩∑S∫d​R​⟨ΨV|R​S⟩​⟨R​S|ΨV⟩,E_{V}=\frac{\langle\Psi_{V}|H|\Psi_{V}\rangle}{\langle\Psi_{V}|\Psi_{V}\rangle}=\frac{\sum_{S}\int dR\,\langle\Psi_{V}|RS\rangle\langle RS|H|\Psi_{V}\rangle}{\sum_{S}\int dR\,\langle\Psi_{V}|RS\rangle\langle RS|\Psi_{V}\rangle}, (3.1)

where, for brevity, we have dropped the explicit dependence of the variational state on a set of parameters 𝜽\boldsymbol{\theta}. Since a deterministic evaluation is computationally prohibitive, these expressions are estimated stochastically using Monte Carlo sampling. To this end, it is convenient to rewrite the variational energy as

EV=∑S∫d​R​|ΨV​(R,S)|2​⟨R​S​|H|​ΨV⟩⟨R​S|ΨV⟩∑S∫d​R​|ΨV​(R,S)|2=∑S∫d​R​πV​(R,S)​EL​(R,S),E_{V}=\frac{\sum_{S}\int dR\,|\Psi_{V}(R,S)|^{2}\dfrac{\langle RS|H|\Psi_{V}\rangle}{\langle RS|\Psi_{V}\rangle}}{\sum_{S}\int dR\,|\Psi_{V}(R,S)|^{2}}=\sum_{S}\int dR\,\pi_{V}(R,S)\,E_{L}(R,S)\,, (3.2)

where we introduced the probability distribution and the local energy,

πV​(R,S)=|ΨV​(R,S)|2∑S∫d​R​|ΨV​(R,S)|2,EL​(R,S)=⟨R​S​|H|​ΨV⟩⟨R​S|ΨV⟩.\pi_{V}(R,S)=\frac{|\Psi_{V}(R,S)|^{2}}{\sum_{S}\int dR\,|\Psi_{V}(R,S)|^{2}}\,,\qquad E_{L}(R,S)=\frac{\langle RS|H|\Psi_{V}\rangle}{\langle RS|\Psi_{V}\rangle}\,. (3.3)

This procedure is unbiased, since configurations with ΨV​(R,S)=0\Psi_{V}(R,S)=0 do not contribute to Eq. (3.1), and the reweighting by |ΨV​(R,S)|2|\Psi_{V}(R,S)|^{2} is therefore well defined.

In most NQS-based applications of the VMC method to the nuclear many-body problem Adams et al. [2021], Gnech et al. [2021], Yang and Zhao [2022], Yang and Zhao [2023], Gnech et al. [2024], with the notable exception of Ref. Wen et al. [2025], the Metropolis–Hastings algorithm Metropolis et al. [1953], Hastings [1970] is used to generate Markov chain samples of spatial and spin–isospin configurations distributed according to πV​(R,S)\pi_{V}(R,S). The resulting NconfN_{\rm conf} configurations are then used to estimate ground-state expectation values via

EV≃1Nconf​∑{R,S}∼πVEL​(R,S).E_{V}\simeq\frac{1}{N_{\rm conf}}\sum_{\{R,S\}\sim\pi_{V}}E_{L}(R,S)\,. (3.4)

The initial 3​A3A spatial coordinates of the nucleons are typically sampled from a Gaussian distribution centered at the origin, with per–coordinate variance chosen to reproduce the target rms point radius. For example, taking Rpt≈1.2​A1/3​fmR_{\rm pt}\approx 1.2\,A^{1/3}\,\mathrm{fm}, one may set σ2=Rpt2/3\sigma^{2}=R_{\rm pt}^{2}/3. The zz-projections of the spin–isospin degrees of freedom are randomly initialized so that the total charge and total spin of the nucleus of interest are reproduced. Each Monte Carlo step consists of a Gaussian move of the 3​A3A spatial coordinates. Since charge is conserved, an ergodic isospin move within fixed ZZ is to swap the isospin labels of a randomly selected pair of nucleons. The same swap is a legitimate move for the spin labels if tensor and spin–orbit contributions in the NN potential are neglected, so that the total spin projection Sz=∑isizS_{z}=\sum_{i}s_{i}^{z} is conserved. However, when tensor or spin–orbit interactions are present, one also needs moves that do not conserve SzS_{z}, such as single or double spin flips, to ensure ergodicity.

The newly proposed spatial configuration R′R^{\prime} and spin–isospin projection S′S^{\prime} are accepted separately (in two successive Metropolis updates) with probabilities

A⁡(R→R′)=min⁡[1,|ΨV​(R′,S)|2|ΨV​(R,S)|2],A⁡(S→S′)=min⁡[1,|ΨV​(R,S′)|2|ΨV​(R,S)|2],A(R\!\to\!R^{\prime})=\min\!\left[1,\frac{|\Psi_{V}(R^{\prime},S)|^{2}}{|\Psi_{V}(R,S)|^{2}}\right],\qquad A(S\!\to\!S^{\prime})=\min\!\left[1,\frac{|\Psi_{V}(R,S^{\prime})|^{2}}{|\Psi_{V}(R,S)|^{2}}\right], (3.5)

where we have assumed symmetric proposal kernels for the Gaussian spatial moves. The width of the Gaussian “kick” is tuned to keep the spatial acceptance rate near 0.60.6.

After NthermN_{\rm therm} thermalization steps, which are necessary to equilibrate the Markov chain, the Metropolis–Hastings algorithm produces configurations {R,S}\{R,S\} distributed according to the target probability πV​(R,S)\pi_{V}(R,S). Because successive samples are correlated, NvoidN_{\rm void} “void” (non-measurement) steps are typically inserted between measurements, and chosen such that the residual autocorrelation falls below a prescribed threshold. After equilibration, a total of NmeasN_{\rm meas} measurements are performed. To improve efficiency, the embarrassingly parallel nature of the Metropolis–Hastings algorithm is exploited by propagating NchainsN_{\rm chains} independent Markov chains in parallel, so that the total number of configurations used to estimate observables is Nconf=Nchains×NmeasN_{\rm conf}=N_{\rm chains}\times N_{\rm meas}.

3.2  Optimization strategies

The energy estimate in Eq. (2.14) provides an upper bound to the ground-state energy. One must still minimize this quantity with respect to the parameters 𝜽\boldsymbol{\theta}, which turns VMC into a nonlinear optimization problem:

E∗=min𝜽⁡EV​(𝜽),𝜽∗=arg⁡min𝜽​EV​(𝜽).E^{*}=\min_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\,E_{V}(\boldsymbol{\theta})\,,\qquad\boldsymbol{\theta}^{*}=\arg\min_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\,E_{V}(\boldsymbol{\theta})\,. (3.6)

A standard strategy is to solve this problem iteratively. A succinct account of such iterative approaches in the NQS setting is given below. For comprehensive treatments in machine learning and optimization (including non-iterative methods), see Refs. Nocedal and Wright [2006], Amari [2016].

In an iterative scheme, one starts from an initial parameter vector 𝜽\boldsymbol{\theta} and updates it as 𝜽←𝜽+𝜹\boldsymbol{\theta}\leftarrow\boldsymbol{\theta}+\boldsymbol{\delta}, where the increment 𝜹\boldsymbol{\delta} is chosen to reduce the energy objective. In the NQS setting, a common choice is

𝜹=−η​S−1​𝐠,\boldsymbol{\delta}\;=\;-\,\eta\,S^{-1}\,\mathbf{g}\,, (3.7)

which corresponds to minimizing the local quadratic model

M⁡(𝜹)=EV​(𝜽)+𝜹⊤​𝐠+12​𝜹⊤​S​𝜹.M(\boldsymbol{\delta})\;=\;E_{V}(\boldsymbol{\theta})\;+\;\boldsymbol{\delta}^{\top}\mathbf{g}\;+\;\tfrac{1}{2}\,\boldsymbol{\delta}^{\top}S\,\boldsymbol{\delta}\,. (3.8)

The scalar η\eta is the learning rate that controls the overall step size in parameter space. The gradient of the variational energy is

gi=2​(⟨ΨV|Oi†​H|ΨV⟩⟨ΨV|ΨV⟩−⟨ΨV|Oi†|ΨV⟩⟨ΨV|ΨV⟩​⟨ΨV|H|ΨV⟩⟨ΨV|ΨV⟩),g_{i}=2\left(\frac{\braket{\Psi_{V}|O_{i}^{\dagger}H|\Psi_{V}}}{\braket{\Psi_{V}|\Psi_{V}}}-\frac{\braket{\Psi_{V}|O_{i}^{\dagger}|\Psi_{V}}}{\braket{\Psi_{V}|\Psi_{V}}}\frac{\braket{\Psi_{V}|H|\Psi_{V}}}{\braket{\Psi_{V}|\Psi_{V}}}\right)\!, (3.9)

where Oi​|ΨV​(𝜽)⟩=∂θi|ΨV​(𝜽)⟩O_{i}|\Psi_{V}(\boldsymbol{\theta})\rangle=\partial_{\theta_{i}}|\Psi_{V}(\boldsymbol{\theta})\rangle denotes a derivative of the wave function with respect to i−i-th parameter. The matrix SS serves as a preconditioner, and different optimization schemes prescribe different choices. In the information-geometry paradigm, SS accounts for the curvature and geometry of parameter space, beyond the Euclidean (flat-space) gradient descent corresponding to S=IS=I Amari [2016]. In quadratic optimization, there is also a close relationship between SS and the Hessian of the loss function Nocedal and Wright [2006].

An extension of the information geometry approach in many-body quantum mechanics is the stochastic reconfiguration (SR) method Stokes et al. [2020]. Originally and independently introduced in the QMC literature at the end of the last century Sorella [1998], Sorella [2005], SR translates naturally to the NQS setting. It is commonly justified by minimizing the Fubini–Study distance between an updated NQS state and a small imaginary-time step for energy minimization Sorella [1998], Stokes et al. [2020], Park and Kastoryano [2020]. This leads to identifying SS with the real part of the quantum geometric tensor (QGT),

Si​j\displaystyle S_{ij} =⟨ΨV|Oi†​Oj|ΨV⟩⟨ΨV|ΨV⟩−⟨ΨV|Oi†|ΨV⟩⟨ΨV|ΨV⟩​⟨ΨV|Oj|ΨV⟩⟨ΨV|ΨV⟩.\displaystyle=\frac{\braket{\Psi_{V}|O_{i}^{\dagger}O_{j}|\Psi_{V}}}{\braket{\Psi_{V}|\Psi_{V}}}-\frac{\braket{\Psi_{V}|O_{i}^{\dagger}|\Psi_{V}}}{\braket{\Psi_{V}|\Psi_{V}}}\frac{\braket{\Psi_{V}|O_{j}|\Psi_{V}}}{\braket{\Psi_{V}|\Psi_{V}}}\,. (3.10)

The QGT acts as a metric under the Fubini–Study distance Stokes et al. [2020], Park and Kastoryano [2020] and thus encodes the curvature of the manifold of normalized wave functions Dash et al. [2025]. Moreover, for real, non-negative ansätze, one can write ΨV=p\Psi_{V}=\sqrt{p} with pp the Born probability density. In this case, the QGT reduces to one quarter of the classical Fisher information matrix of pp, a central object in information geometry Amari [2016].

Whatever optimization setting is employed, both formal and numerical issues can affect the update in Eq. (3.7) and thereby hamper convergence. On the formal side, one wants the inverse to be well behaved so as to avoid, for instance, excessively large steps. In many schemes, SS is designed to be symmetric positive semidefinite, but it can be ill conditioned or rank deficient. A common remedy is to add a small diagonal damping term, S→S+ϵ​IS\to S+\epsilon I with ϵ>0\epsilon>0, which makes the system positive definite. This regularization augments the quadratic model in Eq. (3.8) with the term ϵ2​‖𝜹‖22\tfrac{\epsilon}{2}\,\|\boldsymbol{\delta}\|_{2}^{2}, where ‖𝜹‖2\|\boldsymbol{\delta}\|_{2} is the Euclidean norm of the parameter update, thereby penalizing large displacements and favoring small-norm updates. However, with this simple regularization, all diagonal elements of the SS matrix are shifted by the same amount, neglecting potential order-of-magnitude differences in their typical changes Sorella et al. [2007].

To address this shortcoming, the authors of Ref. Lovato et al. [2022b] introduce an RMSProp-inspired regularization by accumulating an exponentially decaying average of the squared gradients,

𝐯t=β​𝐯t−1+(1−β)​𝐠t2,\mathbf{v}_{t}=\beta\mathbf{v}_{t-1}+(1-\beta)\,\mathbf{g}_{t}^{2}, (3.11)

and modifying the QGT as S→S+ϵ​diag​(𝐯t+10−8)S\to S+\epsilon\,\mathrm{diag}\!\left(\sqrt{\mathbf{v}_{t}}+10^{-8}\right). In the original formulation of the SR algorithm, increasing ϵ\epsilon suppresses the magnitude of the parameter update and rotates it toward the stochastic-gradient direction. In the RMSProp variant, the regularization instead biases the update toward the RMSProp direction, which typically leads to faster and more stable convergence than simple stochastic gradient descent.

Since the Fisher (QGT) matrix is of size Npar×NparN_{\text{par}}\!\times\!N_{\text{par}}, its storage scales as 𝒪⁡(Npar2)\mathcal{O}(N_{\text{par}}^{2}) in memory, which quickly becomes infeasible. One way to overcome this limitation is to use iterative solvers, such as conjugate gradient Neuscamman et al. [2012] or MINRES Drissi et al. [2024], to solve the linear system associated with the SR update. Alternatively, Ref. Chen and Heyl [2024] introduces an accelerated scheme, minSR, which leverages neural tangent kernel ideas to provide highly efficient inversions. Traditional ML preconditioners like K-FAC have also been employed to approximate SS and its inverse Pfau et al. [2020], although they were not originally devised for unsupervised settings such as standard NQS simulations Drissi et al. [2024].

SR is the most common approach for NQS optimization and, as noted above, aligns directly with the information geometry paradigm. However, alternative strategies based on different geometric principles can also be employed. Ref. Drissi et al. [2024] introduces the use of decision geometry within the NQS setting. Decision geometry Dawid [2007] reduces to information geometry for specific choices of scoring rules and can therefore be viewed as a game-theoretic generalization of standard probabilistic optimization schemes. An appealing feature of this framework is the flexibility to choose among different (proper) scoring rules, while still obtaining well-behaved updates with positive semidefinite preconditioning metrics Parry et al. [2012]. A scoring rule tailored to one-dimensional continuous fermion systems showed promising performance in Ref. Drissi et al. [2024], and further explorations for other systems are underway.

Finally, it is worth noting that iterative ML optimizers often exploit the history of the search via a momentum term: the update δ\delta from iteration k−1k\!-\!1 is stored so that the update at iteration kk depends on both the current gradient and the previous step. Momentum-based schemes used in NQS include variants of RMSProp Park and Kastoryano [2020], Keeble and Rios [2020]. By contrast, standard choices widely used in other neural-network contexts (e.g., stochastic gradient descent or Adam Kingma and Ba [2014]) can be insufficient to achieve the percent-level accuracy typically required for ground-state energies in NQS. A recent example that incorporates step history in a natural-gradient setting is the Subsampled Projected-Increment Natural Gradient (SPRING) method Goldshlager et al. [2024]. In this approach, the quadratic model of Eq. (3.8) is augmented with a term ϵ2​‖𝜹−μ​𝜹prev‖22\tfrac{\epsilon}{2}\,\|\boldsymbol{\delta}-\mu\,\boldsymbol{\delta}_{\mathrm{prev}}\|_{2}^{2}, where 𝜹prev\boldsymbol{\delta}_{\mathrm{prev}} denotes the previous parameter update and μ<1\mu<1 is a damping factor. This proximal term is centered at μ​𝜹prev\mu\,\boldsymbol{\delta}_{\mathrm{prev}}, pulling the new step toward the previous one rather than merely penalizing its magnitude.

3.3  Basics of deep learning

In nuclear physics, the simultaneous treatment of continuous spatial degrees of freedom and discrete spin and isospin degrees of freedom typically requires deep neural architectures composed of multiple multilayer perceptrons (MLPs). These individual MLPs are interconnected in structured ways to enforce the physical symmetries of the quantum many-body system. MLPs are widely recognized as one of the most prominent forms of artificial neural networks (ANN), primarily due to their training simplicity and scalability. However, they can be prone to overfitting in situations where a large data set cannot be made available. VMC-NQS is less prone to this issue, since the number of Monte Carlo samples used to estimate the energy can be increased to improve the effective training set.

A multilayer perceptron is a type of deep feedforward neural network defined by alternating compositions of affine transformations and simple, nonlinear transformations. It consists of an input layer, at least one hidden layer, and an output layer, all of which are densely connected to the adjacent layers only. As the name implies, information flows only in one direction, starting from the input layer and ending at the output layer. For an MLP with LL layers (including the hidden and output layers, but excluding the input layer), we define the layers as

𝒉(0)\displaystyle\boldsymbol{h}^{(0)} =𝒗∈ℝd0,\displaystyle=\boldsymbol{v}\;\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{0}}, (3.12)
𝒉(ℓ)\displaystyle\boldsymbol{h}^{(\ell)} =fℓ(W(ℓ)𝒉(ℓ−1)+𝒃(ℓ))∈ℝdℓ,forℓ=1,…,L,\displaystyle=f_{\ell}\!\left(W^{(\ell)}\boldsymbol{h}^{(\ell-1)}+\boldsymbol{b}^{(\ell)}\right)\;\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\ell}},\hskip 14.22636pt\mathrm{for}\ \ell=1,\dots,L, (3.13)

where 𝒗\boldsymbol{v} denotes the vector of visible nodes for the input layer 𝒉(0)\boldsymbol{h}^{(0)}; 𝒉(ℓ)\boldsymbol{h}^{(\ell)} are the hidden layers for ℓ=1,…,L−1\ell=1,\dots,L-1; 𝒉(L)\boldsymbol{h}^{(L)} is the output layer; and fℓf_{\ell} represents the nonlinear activation function in the ℓ\ell-th layer. Each hidden layer has dimension dℓd_{\ell}, meaning W(ℓ)W^{(\ell)} is a dℓ×dℓ−1d_{\ell}\times d_{\ell-1} weight matrix and 𝒃(ℓ)\boldsymbol{b}^{(\ell)} is a dℓd_{\ell}-dimensional bias vector. The activation functions fℓf_{\ell} introduce nonlinearity to the network, enabling it to learn and approximate complex functions. Without at least one nonlinear activation function, the neural network reduces to a purely linear model. In NQS applications for continuous-space systems, the activation functions in the hidden layers should be at least twice continuously differentiable to enable the stable computation of the local kinetic energy. If the target space is unbounded, the activation function for the output layer fLf_{L} is usually chosen to be the identity.

Gradients of MLPs with respect to the weights W(ℓ)W^{(\ell)} and biases 𝒃(ℓ)\boldsymbol{b}^{(\ell)} are efficiently computed through backpropagation, which applies the chain rule recursively:

∂𝒉(L)∂W(ℓ)=(∏k=ℓ+1L∂𝒉(k)∂𝒉(k−1))​∂𝒉(ℓ)∂W(ℓ),∂𝒉(L)∂𝒃(ℓ)=(∏k=ℓ+1L∂𝒉(k)∂𝒉(k−1))​∂𝒉(ℓ)∂𝒃(ℓ).\displaystyle\frac{\partial\boldsymbol{h}^{(L)}}{\partial W^{(\ell)}}=\left(\prod_{k=\ell+1}^{L}\frac{\partial\boldsymbol{h}^{(k)}}{\partial\boldsymbol{h}^{(k-1)}}\right)\frac{\partial\boldsymbol{h}^{(\ell)}}{\partial W^{(\ell)}},\ \ \ \ \ \frac{\partial\boldsymbol{h}^{(L)}}{\partial\boldsymbol{b}^{(\ell)}}=\left(\prod_{k=\ell+1}^{L}\frac{\partial\boldsymbol{h}^{(k)}}{\partial\boldsymbol{h}^{(k-1)}}\right)\frac{\partial\boldsymbol{h}^{(\ell)}}{\partial\boldsymbol{b}^{(\ell)}}. (3.14)

In deep architectures, the repeated multiplication of layer Jacobians can cause gradients to vanish or explode, as the eigenvalues of these matrices can be much smaller or larger than unity. Modern architectures mitigate this effect through skip connections, which facilitate gradient flow by providing alternative paths for information propagation. Two common forms are the residual skip connection,

𝒉(ℓ+1)=𝒉(ℓ)+Fℓ​(𝒉(ℓ)),\boldsymbol{h}^{(\ell+1)}=\boldsymbol{h}^{(\ell)}+F_{\ell}\!\left(\boldsymbol{h}^{(\ell)}\right), (3.15)

and the concatenative skip connection,

𝒉(ℓ+1)=concat⁡(𝒉(ℓ),Fℓ​(𝒉(ℓ))),\boldsymbol{h}^{(\ell+1)}=\mathrm{concat}\!\left(\boldsymbol{h}^{(\ell)},\ F_{\ell}\!\left(\boldsymbol{h}^{(\ell)}\right)\right), (3.16)

where FℓF_{\ell} typically denotes a feedforward transformation (e.g. an MLP block). The additive, or residual, form preserves dimensionality and is widely used for stabilizing deep networks, while the concatenative form aggregates intermediate features, allowing later layers to access information from all previous representations.

To represent complex wave functions using deep neural networks with real parameters, one possible strategy is to predict the real and imaginary parts of the wave function separately, for instance using two output nodes in the final layer or two distinct networks. However, optimization is typically more stable when the network instead predicts the log-amplitude log⁡|ΨV|\log|\Psi_{V}| and phase ΦV=arg⁡(ΨV)\Phi_{V}=\arg(\Psi_{V}). In this parameterization, ΨV=elog⁡|ΨV|+i​ΦV,\Psi_{V}=e^{\log|\Psi_{V}|+i\Phi_{V}}, the log-derivative reduces to ∇logΨV=∇log|ΨV|+i∇ΦV\nabla\log\Psi_{V}=\nabla\log|\Psi_{V}|+i\,\nabla\Phi_{V}, so that the quantities entering the VMC estimators are directly given by smooth network outputs. This leads to numerically well-behaved gradients and reduces the risk of vanishing or exploding updates during training.

A major advantage of deep neural networks is their flexibility to incorporate physical symmetries directly into the architecture. For systems of identical particles, the wave function must be symmetric under particle exchange for bosons and antisymmetric for fermions. In both cases, it is useful to construct permutation-invariant components so that the network naturally treats particles as indistinguishable, without requiring explicit handling of all possible particle permutations, whose number grows factorially with system size. The Deep Sets Zaheer et al. [2017] construction provides a simple way to build such invariant representations,

f⁡({𝐱i}i=1A)=ρ⁡(pool⁡({ϕ⁡(𝐱i)}i=1A)),f(\{\mathbf{x}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{A})=\rho\!\left(\mathrm{pool}\!\left(\{\phi(\mathbf{x}_{i})\}_{i=1}^{A}\right)\right), (3.17)

where 𝐱i=(𝐫i,siz,tiz)\mathbf{x}_{i}=(\mathbf{r}_{i},s_{i}^{z},t_{i}^{z}) denotes the single-particle degrees of freedom of the iith nucleon; ϕ\phi and ρ\rho are learnable maps; and pool\mathrm{pool} is a permutation-invariant aggregation operation (e.g., sum, mean, or logsumexp). Here, ϕ\phi embeds each element of the set into a higher-dimensional latent space, pool\mathrm{pool} combines all elements into a single latent representation of the set, and ρ\rho maps this representation to the desired output space. This construction can be applied similarly to the set of all pairwise degrees of freedom.

A wide range of architectural components can be incorporated to further enhance the flexibility and expressive power of neural networks. One prominent example is the use of attention mechanisms Vaswani et al. [2017], which dynamically weigh the importance of different elements in an input sequence when making predictions. Instead of processing all input features equally, attention allows the network to focus selectively on the most relevant parts, effectively learning context-dependent weighting. They form the foundation of modern large language models, enabling them to capture long-range dependencies and nuanced contextual relationships, and have recently been incorporated into neural quantum state architectures to enhance the representation of complex correlations in many-body wavefunctions von Glehn et al. [2022], Pescia et al. [2024], Geier et al. [2025].

The standard formulation of the self-attention mechanism Vaswani et al. [2017] computes queries, keys and values for each element of the input through linear transformations,

Q=X​WQ,K=X​WK,V=X​WV.Q=XW_{Q},\hskip 28.45274ptK=XW_{K},\hskip 28.45274ptV=XW_{V}. (3.18)

As a minimal example, consider the input matrix X∈ℝA×5X\in\mathbb{R}^{A\times 5}, chosen to represent the row-wise collection of all single-nucleon degrees of freedom, corresponding to the three spatial coordinates together with the spin and isospin labels. One could alternatively construct XX to represent pair degrees of freedom or, more generally, the output of a preceding neural network layer. Choosing the query and key weight matrices WQW_{Q} and WKW_{K} to have dimension 5×dk5\times d_{k}, the value weight matrix WVW_{V} will have dimension 5×dv5\times d_{v}, yielding Q,K∈ℝA×dkQ,K\in\mathbb{R}^{A\times d_{k}} and V∈ℝA×dvV\in\mathbb{R}^{A\times d_{v}}. The output of the attention layer is obtained by comparing the query of each particle with the keys of all others, producing a set of normalized weights that are then applied to the values to generate a context-aware representation,

attn⁡(Q,K,V)=softmaxi​(Q​KTdk)​V.\mathrm{attn}(Q,K,V)=\mathrm{softmax}_{i}\!\left(\frac{QK^{T}}{\sqrt{d_{k}}}\right)V. (3.19)

The intermediate matrix Q​KT∈ℝA×AQK^{T}\in\mathbb{R}^{A\times A} encodes all pairwise similarities between particles and is effectively bilinear in XX. The row-wise softmaxi\mathrm{softmax}_{i} activation function converts each row into a normalized probability distribution, and the factor of 1/dk1/\sqrt{d_{k}} aids numerical stability.

3.4  Wave function ansätze

Here we review the principal wave function ansätze that have been used in “first-quantized” NQS approaches to nuclear physics. These architectures act directly on the continuous spatial coordinates and spin–isospin degrees of freedom of the nucleons.

3.4.1  Slater–Jastrow

Initial applications of the NQS framework to atomic nuclei Adams et al. [2021] extended the Slater–Jastrow (SJ) architecture, originally developed for quantum chemistry Hermann et al. [2020], Pfau et al. [2020], to handle the complex spin–isospin structure of nuclear interactions. Such an ansatz can be schematically written as

ΨSJ​(X)=F⁡(X)​Φ​(X),\Psi_{\rm SJ}(X)=F(X)\,\Phi(X)\,, (3.20)

where F⁡(X)F(X) is a permutation-invariant Jastrow factor, and antisymmetry is enforced by the mean-field-like component Φ⁡(X)\Phi(X). For compactness, we use X=(x1,…,xA)X=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{A}) to denote the collection of all single-particle degrees of freedom xi=(𝐫i,siz,tiz)x_{i}=(\mathbf{r}_{i},s_{i}^{z},t_{i}^{z}), namely the three-dimensional spatial coordinates 𝐫i\mathbf{r}_{i} and the spin and isospin projections along the zz-axis.

The mean-field term Φ⁡(X)\Phi(X) is typically expressed as a sum of Slater determinants of single-particle orbitals Adams et al. [2021], Gnech et al. [2020], Yang and Zhao [2022]. For atomic nuclei, it takes the form

Φ(X)=[∑μCμ𝒜[ϕα1μ(x1)ϕα2μ(x2)⋯ϕαAμ(xA)]]Jπ​T,\Phi(X)=\Bigg[\sum_{\mu}C_{\mu}\,\mathcal{A}\!\left[\phi_{\alpha_{1}^{\mu}}(x_{1})\,\phi_{\alpha_{2}^{\mu}}(x_{2})\cdots\phi_{\alpha_{A}^{\mu}}(x_{A})\right]\Bigg]_{J^{\pi}T}\!, (3.21)

where 𝒜\mathcal{A} is the antisymmetrization operator acting on the particle labels xix_{i}, and {Cμ}\{C_{\mu}\} are configuration amplitudes that incorporate the Clebsch–Gordan couplings required to form a many-body state μ\mu with the desired total angular momentum, parity, and isospin Jπ​TJ^{\pi}T for the nucleus of interest. The single-particle orbitals are evaluated as

ϕα​(xi)=ℛn​l​(ri)​Yl​lz​(r^i)​⟨siz|sz⟩​⟨tiz|tz⟩,\phi_{\alpha}(x_{i})=\mathcal{R}_{nl}(r_{i})\,Y_{l\,l^{z}}(\hat{r}_{i})\,\langle s_{i}^{z}|s^{z}\rangle\,\langle t_{i}^{z}|t^{z}\rangle\,, (3.22)

where α=(n,l,lz,sz,tz)\alpha=(n,l,l^{z},s^{z},t^{z}) are the quantum numbers, ⟨siz|sz⟩=δsiz,sz\langle s_{i}^{z}|s^{z}\rangle=\delta_{s_{i}^{z},s^{z}} and ⟨tiz|tz⟩=δtiz,tz\langle t_{i}^{z}|t^{z}\rangle=\delta_{t_{i}^{z},t^{z}} project onto the fixed spin and isospin, ℛn​l​(ri)\mathcal{R}_{nl}(r_{i}) are the radial functions parametrized by MLPs, and Yl​lz​(r^i)Y_{l\,l^{z}}(\hat{r}_{i}) are the spherical harmonics.

To automatically remove the spurious center-of-mass contribution from the kinetic energy, the spatial coordinates are replaced by 𝐫i→𝐫i−𝐑CM\mathbf{r}_{i}\to\mathbf{r}_{i}-\mathbf{R}_{\rm CM}, with 𝐑CM=1A​∑i=1A𝐫i\mathbf{R}_{\rm CM}=\frac{1}{A}\sum_{i=1}^{A}\mathbf{r}_{i} being the center-of-mass coordinate Massella et al. [2020]. Since the network parameters are randomly initialized, in the early stages of training the Metropolis–Hastings walk can let the nucleons drift away from 𝐑CM\mathbf{R}_{\mathrm{CM}}. To control this behavior, a Gaussian factor is multiplied by the single-particle radial functions to confine the nucleons within a finite volume,

ℛn​l​(ri)→ℛn​l​(ri)​e−α​ri2.\mathcal{R}_{nl}(r_{i})\;\to\;\mathcal{R}_{nl}(r_{i})\,e^{-\alpha r_{i}^{2}}\,. (3.23)

Typical values for the confining constant are in the range α=0.02\alpha=0.02–0.05​fm−20.05~\text{fm}^{-2}.

In Refs. Adams et al. [2021], Gnech et al. [2020], Yang and Zhao [2022], the real-valued Jastrow correlator was taken to be of the form

F⁡(X)=e𝒰⁡(X)​tanh⁡[𝒱⁡(X)].\displaystyle F(X)=e^{\mathcal{U}(X)}\,\tanh\!\big[\mathcal{V}(X)\big]\,. (3.24)

Here, the positive-definite exponential is modulated by a hyperbolic tangent, which acts as a smooth surrogate for the sign. The functions 𝒰⁡(X)\mathcal{U}(X) and 𝒱⁡(X)\mathcal{V}(X) are implemented as permutation-invariant neural networks. Several architectures have been developed to represent such functions efficiently, including point-cloud Charles et al. [2017] and attention-based Vinyals et al. [2015], Vaswani et al. [2017], Lee et al. [2018] models. Among these, the authors of Ref. Adams et al. [2021] found the Deep Sets architecture Zaheer et al. [2017], Wagstaff et al. [2019] to be a practical and sufficiently accurate choice, discussed further in Section 3.3.

In particular, each single-particle input xix_{i} is mapped independently to a latent representation, and a sum aggregation is applied to enforce permutation invariance:

𝒰⁡(X)=ρ𝒰​(∑i=1Aϕ𝒰​(xi)),𝒱⁡(X)=ρ𝒱​(∑i=1Aϕ𝒱​(xi)).\mathcal{U}(X)=\rho_{\mathcal{U}}\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^{A}\phi_{\mathcal{U}}(x_{i})\right),\qquad\mathcal{V}(X)=\rho_{\mathcal{V}}\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^{A}\phi_{\mathcal{V}}(x_{i})\right). (3.25)

Both ϕ𝒰\phi_{\mathcal{U}} and ρ𝒰\rho_{\mathcal{U}} (and analogously ϕ𝒱\phi_{\mathcal{V}} and ρ𝒱\rho_{\mathcal{V}}) are typically implemented as MLPs. Computing the kinetic energy (Laplacian) requires activation functions that are differentiable (ideally twice). Standard choices include hyperbolic tangent, softplus Dugas et al. [2001], and GELU Hendrycks and Gimpel [2023].

Instead of single-particle inputs as in Ref. Adams and others [2021], Ref. Gnech et al. [2020] maps the coordinates of each particle pair directly to a latent-space representation, in close analogy with earlier condensed-matter applications Pfau et al. [2020], Hermann et al. [2020]. As before, a sum aggregation removes any dependence on particle ordering and therefore enforces permutation invariance:

𝒰⁡(X)=ρ𝒰​(∑i≠jϕ𝒰​(xi,xj)),𝒱⁡(X)=ρ𝒱​(∑i≠jϕ𝒱​(xi,xj)).\mathcal{U}(X)=\rho_{\mathcal{U}}\!\left(\sum_{i\neq j}\phi_{\mathcal{U}}(x_{i},x_{j})\right),\qquad\mathcal{V}(X)=\rho_{\mathcal{V}}\!\left(\sum_{i\neq j}\phi_{\mathcal{V}}(x_{i},x_{j})\right). (3.26)

When single-particle coordinates are used as input, correlations are generated in the latent feature space by the aggregation network ρℱ\rho_{\mathcal{F}}, where we use ℱ∈{𝒰,𝒱}\mathcal{F}\in\{\mathcal{U},\mathcal{V}\} to denote either of the two correlator networks. By contrast, using pair coordinates introduces correlations already at the level of the real-space inputs. The conventional two-body Jastrow ansatz is recovered when the latent dimension is one and ρℱ\rho_{\mathcal{F}} is taken to be the identity, ρℱ​(x)=x\rho_{\mathcal{F}}(x)=x. In a similar spirit, Ref. Yang and Zhao [2022] feeds only rotationally invariant one- and two-body features to ϕ𝒰\phi_{\mathcal{U}} and ϕ𝒱\phi_{\mathcal{V}}, namely ‖𝐫i‖\|\mathbf{r}_{i}\|, ‖𝐫j‖\|\mathbf{r}_{j}\|, and ‖𝐫i−𝐫j‖\|\mathbf{r}_{i}-\mathbf{r}_{j}\|, while neglecting spin–isospin dependence. This choice significantly reduces the number of variational parameters without compromising the accuracy of the resulting energies.

3.4.2  Operator-dependent Slater–Jastrow

Very recently, VMC methods based on NQS Yang et al. [2025b], Yang et al. [2025a], Wen et al. [2025] have been applied to the nuclear many-body problem using high-resolution phenomenological and chiral-EFT Hamiltonians that are local in coordinate space. To address the strongly non-perturbative character of these interactions, in particular their tensor component, the NQS includes explicit spin–isospin operator dependence, as in Eq. (2.15). To keep a polynomial computational cost in the number of nucleons, the ansatz introduced in Ref. Yang et al. [2025b] is expressed in the same linearized form used in AFDMC, reported in Eq. (2.20), namely

ΨV​(R,S)=e𝒰​(R)​tanh⁡[𝒱⁡(R)]​(1+∑i<j∑p=16Wi​jp​(R)​Oi​jp).\Psi_{V}(R,S)=e^{\mathcal{U}}(R)\tanh[\mathcal{V}(R)]\left(1+\sum_{i<j}\sum_{p=1}^{6}W^{p}_{ij}(R)O^{p}_{ij}\right). (3.27)

As a reminder, the first six spin-isospin operators are Oi​jp=1,6=(1,τi​j,σi​j,σi​j​τi​j,Si​j,Si​j​τi​j)O^{p=1,6}_{ij}=\bigl(1,\tau_{ij},\sigma_{ij},\sigma_{ij}\tau_{ij},S_{ij},S_{ij}\tau_{ij}\bigr). The central correlation functions 𝒰⁡(R)\mathcal{U}(R) and 𝒱⁡(R)\mathcal{V}(R) are represented by the spin–isospin independent permutation-invariant neural network of Eq. (3.26), introduced in Ref. Yang and Zhao [2022]. Importantly, this construction ensures both translational and rotational invariance.

Contrary to conventional GFMC and AFDMC trial wave functions, in which the pair correlation functions Wi​jpW^{p}_{ij} depend only on the relative coordinate of particles ii and jj, the present ansatz makes Wi​jpW^{p}_{ij} a functional of the full configuration RR. This is achieved using the Deep Sets architecture, discussed above and in Section 3.3, which incorporates information from all particles through

Wi​jp​(R)=ρ𝒲p​(∑k=1Aϕ𝒲​(ri​k,rj​k,ri​j)),W^{p}_{ij}(R)=\rho_{\mathcal{W}}^{p}\!\left(\sum_{k=1}^{A}\phi_{\mathcal{W}}(r_{ik},r_{jk},r_{ij})\right), (3.28)

where ϕ𝒲\phi_{\mathcal{W}} and ρ𝒲\rho_{\mathcal{W}} are feedforward neural networks, each with a single fully connected hidden layer. This global dependence allows the pair correlations to adapt to the surrounding many-body environment. As a result, these wave functions provide an excellent starting point for GFMC calculations and were used in Ref. Yang et al. [2025b] to compute peripheral neutron–α\alpha scattering with high accuracy. A more detailed discussion of these results is given in Section 4.5.

A similar ansatz, but incorporating the symmetrized product of two-body correlations—see Eq. (2.15) for its conventional counterpart—has been proposed by the authors of Ref. Wen et al. [2025]:

ΨV​(R,S)=(1+∑i<j<kFi​j​k)​∏i<jfi​jc​(R)​(1+∑p=26ui​jp​(R)​Oi​jp).\Psi_{V}(R,S)=\left(1+\sum_{i<j<k}F_{ijk}\right)\prod_{i<j}f^{c}_{ij}(R)\left(1+\sum_{p=2}^{6}u_{ij}^{p}(R)\,O_{ij}^{p}\right). (3.29)

The three-body correlation functions Fi​j​kF_{ijk} are defined analogously to Eq. (2.17). As in the ansatz of Ref. Wen et al. [2025], all radial functions entering the two- and three-body correlations depend on the full configuration RR. A representative example is the operator-dependent correlation,

ui​jp​(R)=ρup​(ri​j,∑k≠i,j[ϕu​(ri​j)+ϕu​(ri​k)]),u_{ij}^{p}(R)=\rho_{u}^{p}\!\left(r_{ij},\,\sum_{k\neq i,j}\left[\,\phi_{u}(r_{ij})+\phi_{u}(r_{ik})\,\right]\right), (3.30)

where both ρup\rho_{u}^{p} and ϕu\phi_{u} are feed-forward neural networks composed of multiple one-dimensional transformation layers connected by residual blocks and employing the RiLU activation function.

An important difference from previous NQS implementations is that this approach leverages normalizing flows to produce uncorrelated samples to solve the nuclear Schrödinger equation, as opposed to Metropolis–Hastings sampling. As a consequence, it avoids the autocorrelation issues inherent in Metropolis–Hastings and reduces the overall computational cost. Normalizing flows Albergo et al. [2019], Brady et al. [2021], Wen et al. [2024] generate samples by drawing an initial batch from a simple uniform distribution, implemented here using a Sobol quasi-random sequence, and passing it through a series of invertible change-of-variable transformations with tractable derivatives and Jacobians. By optimizing the parameters of the flow, the resulting distribution can be made to closely approximate the target distribution. Results for the A=3A=3 nuclei obtained with this ansatz and the local chiral-EFT interactions of Ref. Gezerlis et al. [2014] will also be summarized in Section 4.5.

3.4.3  Hidden Nucleons

A systematically improvable family of variational wave functions for strongly correlated fermionic systems was introduced in Ref. Moreno et al. [2022]. These wave functions are built from Slater determinants in an augmented Hilbert space that includes additional, “hidden” fermionic degrees of freedom. The authors demonstrated that this ansatz is universal on the lattice and applied it to the ground-state properties of the Hubbard model on the square lattice, achieving accuracies competitive with state-of-the-art variational methods. This framework was subsequently extended to nuclear systems, whose Hilbert spaces involve both continuous and discrete degrees of freedom Lovato et al. [2022b]. In this formulation, the Hilbert space includes fictitious coordinates for AhA_{h} Hidden Nucleons (HN), defined as functions of the visible coordinates Xh=f⁡(X)X_{h}=f(X). The amplitudes of the HN wave function in the XX basis can be written schematically as

ΨHN​(X)≡det[Φv​(X)Φv​(Xh)χh​(X)χh​(Xh)],\Psi_{\rm HN}(X)\equiv\det\begin{bmatrix}\Phi_{v}(X)&\Phi_{v}(X_{h})\\ \chi_{h}(X)&\chi_{h}(X_{h})\\ \end{bmatrix}, (3.31)

where Φv​(X)\Phi_{v}(X) denotes the A×AA\times A matrix of visible single-particle orbitals evaluated at the visible coordinates, equivalent to the mean-field term Φ⁡(X)\Phi(X) of Eq. (3.21). This would be the only component of the wave function in a Hartree–Fock description. In contrast to the original implementation of Ref. Moreno et al. [2022], the columns of the matrix in Eq. (3.31) correspond to different particles, while the rows correspond to different single-particle states. The Ah×AhA_{h}\times A_{h} matrix χh​(Xh)\chi_{h}(X_{h}) contains the amplitudes of hidden orbitals evaluated at hidden coordinates, whereas χh​(X)\chi_{h}(X) and Φv​(Xh)\Phi_{v}(X_{h}) provide the amplitudes of hidden orbitals at visible coordinates and visible orbitals at hidden coordinates, respectively. The SJ ansatz of Eq. (3.20) is recovered in the limit Ah=1A_{h}=1, χh​(X)=0\chi_{h}(X)=0, and Φv​(Xh)=0\Phi_{v}(X_{h})=0, allowing one to interpret it as a special case of the HN formulation. If the function ff is permutation invariant, ΨHN​(X)\Psi_{\rm HN}(X) is automatically antisymmetric under particle exchange. The expressivity of this construction for discrete degrees of freedom was formally proven in Ref. Moreno et al. [2022], provided that the functions χh\chi_{h} and ff are sufficiently general. To avoid the combinatorial complexity of ff, the ii-th columns of Φv​(Xh)\Phi_{v}(X_{h}) and χh​(Xh)\chi_{h}(X_{h}) are parametrized by independent, permutation-invariant neural networks as

Φvi​(Xh)=e𝒰Φi​(X)​tanh⁡[𝒱Φi​(X)],χhi​(Xh)=e𝒰χi​(X)​tanh⁡[𝒱χi​(X)].\Phi_{v}^{i}(X_{h})=e^{\mathcal{U}^{i}_{\Phi}(X)}\tanh[\mathcal{V}^{i}_{\Phi}(X)],\qquad\chi_{h}^{i}(X_{h})=e^{\mathcal{U}^{i}_{\chi}(X)}\tanh[\mathcal{V}^{i}_{\chi}(X)]. (3.32)

A more recent implementations of the HN ansatz Gnech et al. [2024] employs complex-valued matrices of the form

Φvi​(Xh)=e𝒰Φi​(X)+i​𝒱Φi​(X),χhi​(Xh)=e𝒰χi​(X)+i​𝒱χi​(X).\Phi_{v}^{i}(X_{h})=e^{\mathcal{U}^{i}_{\Phi}(X)+i\mathcal{V}^{i}_{\Phi}(X)},\qquad\chi_{h}^{i}(X_{h})=e^{\mathcal{U}^{i}_{\chi}(X)+i\mathcal{V}^{i}_{\chi}(X)}. (3.33)

In both formulations, permutation invariance is enforced using Deep Sets architectures Zaheer et al. [2017], Wagstaff et al. [2019] to express the functions 𝒰Φi\mathcal{U}^{i}_{\Phi}, 𝒱Φi\mathcal{V}^{i}_{\Phi}, 𝒰χi\mathcal{U}^{i}_{\chi}, and 𝒱χi\mathcal{V}^{i}_{\chi}. For applications to finite nuclei Lovato et al. [2022b] and dilute neutron matter Fore et al. [2023], a logsumexp\mathrm{logsumexp} pooling operation replaces the simple sums in Eqs. (3.25) and (3.26),

ℱ⁡(X)=ρℱ​[log⁡(∑ieϕℱ​(xi))].\mathcal{F}(X)=\rho_{\mathcal{F}}\left[\log\Big(\sum_{i}e^{\phi_{\mathcal{F}}(x_{i})}\Big)\right]\,. (3.34)

In these works, ϕℱ\phi_{\mathcal{F}} and ρℱ\rho_{\mathcal{F}} are implemented as MLPs with two hidden layers of 16 nodes each, and a 16-dimensional latent space connecting them. The output layers of ρℱ\rho_{\mathcal{F}} contain AA nodes for ℱ=𝒰Φi,𝒱Φi\mathcal{F}=\mathcal{U}^{i}_{\Phi},\mathcal{V}^{i}_{\Phi} and AhA_{h} nodes for ℱ=𝒰χi,𝒱χi\mathcal{F}=\mathcal{U}^{i}_{\chi},\mathcal{V}^{i}_{\chi}. An ablation study in Ref. Lovato et al. [2022b] examined the convergence of the 4He ground-state energy with network size and found that increasing the number of hidden layers or nodes beyond this configuration provided no substantial improvement, while smaller networks slightly degraded the accuracy (by about 0.2 MeV). The single-particle orbitals defining Φv​(X)\Phi_{v}(X) and χh​(X)\chi_{h}(X) are also represented by MLPs that take as input the single-particle coordinates xix_{i}. In Refs. Lovato et al. [2022b], Fore et al. [2023], these networks had two hidden layers with ten nodes each, tanh\tanh activation functions, and one-dimensional linear outputs. Other differentiable activations such as softplus\mathrm{softplus} and GELU\mathrm{GELU} were tested without appreciable differences. Differentiability is required to compute the kinetic energy, which involves second derivatives of the wave function. Unlike in the Slater–Jastrow case, confinement is not imposed at the single-particle level. Instead, the full wave function in Eq. (3.31) is multiplied by a global Gaussian factor,

ΨHN(X)→ΨHN(X),e−α∑i=1Ari2,\Psi_{\rm HN}(X)\to\Psi_{\rm HN}(X),e^{-\alpha\sum_{i=1}^{A}r_{i}^{2}}\,, (3.35)

which ensures spatial localization of the system.

When introducing the HN ansatz, the authors of Ref. Lovato et al. [2022b] found it beneficial to enforce point symmetries, such as parity and time reversal. For positive- and negative-parity states, one can impose

ΨHNP+​(X)\displaystyle\Psi_{\rm HN}^{P^{+}}(X) =ΨHN​(R,S)+ΨHN​(−R,S),\displaystyle=\Psi_{\rm HN}(R,S)+\Psi_{\rm HN}(-R,S)\,,
ΨHNP−​(X)\displaystyle\Psi_{\rm HN}^{P^{-}}(X) =ΨHN​(R,S)−ΨHN​(−R,S).\displaystyle=\Psi_{\rm HN}(R,S)-\Psi_{\rm HN}(-R,S)\,. (3.36)

For even-even nuclei, such as 4He and 16O, it is also possible to enforce time-reversal symmetry,

ΨHNT​(X)≡ΨHN​(R,S)+ΨHN∗​(R,θ​S).\displaystyle\Psi_{\rm HN}^{T}(X)\equiv\Psi_{\rm HN}(R,S)+\Psi_{\rm HN}^{*}(R,\theta S)\,. (3.37)

where θ​S\theta S is obtained by applying the operator −i​σy-i\sigma_{y} to all single-particle spinors Bohr and Mottelson [1998]. Note that, unlike the expression reported in Ref. Lovato et al.
